title: One voice of a Prophet-5
intro: The Pro-1 is a copy of the Sequential Circuits Pro-One of 1981, and the Pro-One was one voice taken out of the Prophet-5, the first polyphonic synthesizer that could remember its sounds. So this panel is a close look at a single Prophet voice, with a larger modulation section than the Prophet had room for.

timeline.name: Sequential Circuits
timeline.text: Dave Smith starts the company in San Jose, California, making a digital sequencer and then a programmer that stores knob settings for Moog and ARP synthesizers. Both products are about putting a microprocessor in charge of analogue hardware, which is the idea behind everything that follows.

timeline.name: Prophet-5
timeline.text: Designed by Dave Smith and John Bowen and shown at the NAMM show in January 1978. Five voices, each with two oscillators, a four-pole low-pass filter and two ADSR envelopes, all under the control of a microprocessor that scans the keyboard and stores every knob position as a numbered program. Until then a polyphonic synth either had no memories or very limited ones. Its "Poly-Mod" section lets the filter envelope and Oscillator B modulate Oscillator A and the filter: the ancestor of the modulation matrix on this panel.

timeline.name: Synthesizer on a chip
timeline.text: Doug Curtis’s company, Curtis Electromusic, puts a complete oscillator (the CEM3340) and a complete filter (the CEM3320) on single chips. They hold their tuning far better than hand-built circuits. The Prophet-5 moves to them for its "Rev 3" version, and they also turn up in instruments from Oberheim, Roland and Moog.

timeline.name: Sequential Pro-One
timeline.text: A monophonic synth built from the same Curtis chips as a Prophet-5 Rev 3 voice, at about a sixth of the price. Because there is only one voice, Sequential could afford to expand the modulation: three sources (filter envelope, Oscillator B, LFO), each sent either directly or through the mod wheel, to five destinations. It adds a small sequencer, an arpeggiator, oscillator sync, and a DRONE and REPEAT mode. Around 10,000 were sold before it was dropped in 1984.

timeline.name: MIDI
timeline.text: Dave Smith proposes a universal digital connection between synthesizers at the 1981 AES convention, then works with Roland’s Ikutaro Kakehashi to turn it into MIDI. At the NAMM show in January 1983 a Sequential Prophet-600 and a Roland Jupiter-6 are joined by a cable and play each other. The MIDI IN socket on this panel comes from that handshake.

timeline.name: Sequential closes
timeline.text: Squeezed by cheap digital synths, the company is sold to Yamaha. Smith goes on to work on the Korg Wavestation, founds Dave Smith Instruments in 2002, and gets the Sequential name back in 2015. He reissued the Prophet-5 in 2020 and died in 2022.

timeline.name: Behringer Pro-1
timeline.text: Behringer rebuilds the Pro-One voice around modern copies of the 3340 oscillator and 3320 filter chips, in a desktop case that also fits a Eurorack frame. The panel layout follows the original closely. The additions are the row of patch jacks along the top, MIDI and USB.

relatives.name: Sequential Prophet-5 and Prophet-10
relatives.text: The same voice, five or ten times over, with patch memory. If a record used a Prophet-5 for a mono line, a Pro-One gets very close.

relatives.name: Sequential Prophet-600
relatives.text: A cheaper six-voice Prophet and the first synthesizer sold with MIDI.

relatives.name: Oberheim OB-Xa, Roland SH-101 and Jupiter-6, Memorymoog
relatives.text: Not relations by design, but they share the CEM3340 oscillator chip, which is part of why early-80s synths have a family resemblance. The Neutron in this app uses the same oscillator design.

relatives.name: Moog Prodigy, Roland SH-101
relatives.text: The Pro-One’s rivals as the affordable mono synth of the early 80s. The Pro-One had the most modulation of the three, which is why it was favoured for percussion and effects.

relatives.name: Sequential Pro 2 and Pro 3
relatives.text: Dave Smith’s own later mono synths, in the same spirit with far more of everything.

note: The Pro-One was cheap and common, so it appears on many more records than anyone wrote down. This list keeps to uses that are well documented.
